scenes.synopsis: the instruction, sent — Quill receives his orders; the money, under observation.
scenes.prose:
> *(She sends for Quill at dawn, and gives him the instruction in the study, plainly. Her choice — chase, watch, or bluff — becomes his orders, and he writes them down in the solicitor's hand, which makes them real. "Carefully," she says again. "Always," he says. He pauses at the door. "Miss Hartwell. One thing. If the money is managed, and it is, then the manager knows it's being looked at, whether you chase, watch, or bluff. Managed money feels the attention." He touches his hat. "That's not a warning. That's the point." He goes, the leather case under his arm, carrying the week's second doctrine into the fog.)*
> *(She stands at the study window and watches him down the drive. Somewhere in London, a factor's clerk will open a ledger. Somewhere, a woman named Vane will hear — or not hear — that her money is being watched. She touches the mended glove. Stitch by stitch: the wall, the gloves, and now the money's paper trail.)*

scenes.synopsis: the sting — Bell's draft: "THE FITTING — On Bought Ink and Borrowed Outrage."
scenes.prose:
> *(The sting arrives with the morning post, in Bell's own hand, marked for Rose's eyes: the proprietor's new draft, and the headline set in type: "THE FITTING — On Bought Ink and Borrowed Outrage." Three paragraphs, cool as spring water. They describe, without naming, a gutter sheet that prints blind items for a hundred pounds; a stranger who writes down ghost stories and French poetry from Derby; and a village that has decided to be in on the joke. The last line is the blade: "The Gazette notes that some outrage is purchased by the pound, like tea. This paper's outrage is its own, and it is not for sale." Bell's rule holds: no names. But the fitting is unmistakable, and it will run when Rose says so.)*
> *(Rose reads it twice and understands the weapon's shape: not a defense, but a fitting — measured, public, and funny at Pounce's expense. The village's counter-intelligence, elevated to print. The stranger's notebook, mocked in advance. She files the draft with the Lash in the drawer: the probe, the answer, the fitting. The blade, sheathed until needed. The week, armed.)*
scenes.sting: THE FITTING — On Bought Ink and Borrowed Outrage.

scenes.synopsis: the blade, discussed — when to run the fitting; Bell's terms, plain.
scenes.prose:
> *(Bell comes at noon, in person this time, and they discuss the blade over the good tea. "It runs when you say," Bell says. "Not before. A fitting fired early is just noise." She ticks the triggers on her fingers. "One: Pounce prints names. Two: the stranger knocks. Three: you decide it's time." She looks at Rose. "My terms, plain: I print what's true. The fitting is true — every word of it happened. The haunting, the Derby poetry, the hundred pounds. When it runs, Pounce can't answer it without admitting the purchase." She stands. "It's your blade, Miss Hartwell. I'm only the arm.")*
> *("The arm," Rose says, "is the whole of it." Bell almost smiles. "Flatterer." At the door she turns. "One more thing. Whoever's paying Pounce — they're not done. A hundred pounds was the advertisement. The story will cost more." She goes, leaving the arithmetic: the advertisement, bought; the story, priced; the blade, waiting. Rose files the terms with the draft. The weapon, understood. The price, coming.)*

scenes.synopsis: undressing — the grey, hung; the glove's mend, examined; the day, unpinned.
scenes.prose:
> *(The bedroom, late. The grey silk comes off and is hung with care; it has done its work and earned its rest. The pearls are coiled, the rope wound. The gloves come last. She holds the left one to the lamp the way she held it that morning: the grandmother's mend, the tiny stitches, even as print, holding. Four lines in a gutter sheet. A stranger pricing a witness. A woman named Vane buying eyes and ears. The mend held through all of it. It will hold through whatever comes next.)*
> *(She lays the gloves beside tomorrow's violet and unpins her hair. The day unpins with it: the blind item, the stranger, the draft, the decisions, the mending hall with its forty pairs. Each pin, laid down. Each fact, kept. She is tired the way a woman is tired after being exactly herself for twelve hours. The lamp lowered. The grey, hung. The mend, holding. The woman, held.)*

fashionChoices.label: Dream in grey
fashionChoices.detail: the siege's color, kept in sleep.

fashionChoices.label: Dream in archive
fashionChoices.detail: the cedar wardrobe, unopened; tomorrow, undressed.

fashionChoices.label: No choosing
fashionChoices.detail: sleep takes what it takes.

scenes.synopsis: the friends' talk — Octavia stays the night; being read, discussed.
scenes.prose:
> *(Octavia arrives at eleven with the chocolate, in her dressing gown, and shuts the door with her foot. "Debrief," she says. "The unofficial one." They sit by the fire. "How does it feel," Octavia asks, "to be read by strangers?" Rose considers. "Like being fitted for a gown by someone who's never seen me." Octavia laughs. "And the fitting?" "They've got the measurements wrong," Rose says. "They think I'm the flinch. I'm the —" she looks for the word, "— I'm the grey." "You're the grey," Octavia agrees. "It's a good color on you.")*
> *("Octavia." "Yes?" "If they come with an offer, money, for the papers, for the story," "They will," Octavia says. "That's the next move. The probe, then the purchase." She sips the chocolate. "When they come, hear everything. Promise nothing. And don't —" "Don't answer on their timetable," Rose finishes. "I know." "You know," Octavia says. "I'm saying it anyway. That's what friends are for." The friends' talk, done. The next move, predicted.)*

scenes.synopsis: the card — a lady's card arrives; Thursday noon; the offer, foreshadowed.
scenes.prose:
> *(The card comes with the morning post, on heavy stock, engraved: "Mrs. Quick. Will call Thursday, at noon, on a matter of business. Acting for interested parties." No address. No crest. Rose holds it a long moment. Octavia predicted the purchase; here is its herald. A lady, acting for interested parties, with a matter of business. The politeness of it is the most alarming thing: no threat, no bluster, just a card, a time, and the phrase "interested parties," which means money.)*
> *(She shows it to Letitia, who reads it and says: "Thursday. Noon. The good tea." The quartermaster, already planning. She shows it to Octavia, who says: "Hear everything. Promise nothing." The friend, already counseling. She puts the card on the desk, beside the Lash, the draft, and Bell's fitting: the week's archive, complete. The probe, the purchase's herald, the blade. Today, noon, the offer. She touches the mended glove. The card, received. The business, coming.)*

scenes.synopsis: the cliffhanger — Thursday noon; Mrs. Quick arrives; the offer, about to be stated.
scenes.prose:
> *(Thursday noon. The knocker sounds exactly on the hour, and Letitia brings her in: a plain woman, forty-five, dark gown, a reticule that looks like it carries documents. She curtsies correctly. "Miss Hartwell. Thank you for receiving me. I act for interested parties." She sits where she's shown, places the reticule on her lap, and folds her hands over it. The composure is total. Rose, in the archive grey, the pearls, the mended gloves, watches her settle.)*
> *("I will be brief," the woman says, "because my instructions are precise, and precision respects your time." She opens the reticule and takes out a single folded paper, which she does not unfold. "There is a story about to be printed. Concerning your family's affairs during the late war." She looks up. The eyes are grey and direct. "I am here to offer you the chance to sell it first." The room is very quiet. The good tea steams, untouched. The offer hangs in the air, unstated, the folded paper unopened. And Rose — who has spent a week learning not to flinch — feels the floor shift under the grey silk.)*

scenes.synopsis: the morning before the call — the house, stationed; Rose, ready.
scenes.prose:
> *(Thursday morning moves at Hartwell the way it moves before a christening or a siege. Letitia has been up since six. The morning room is set: the good tea, the grey silk laid out, the violets dried, the Lash in the drawer where the hunters' paper belongs. Rose stands at the window and watches the lane. Nothing on it yet. The call is at noon. A lady, acting for interested parties, with terms to discuss. She has been turning the coming hour the way she turns everything, and the turning has produced a single clear resolution: hear everything, promise nothing, and do not, on any account, answer on their timetable.)*
> *(She thinks of Octavia's counsel: the messenger is furniture. She thinks of Bell: four lines is the fitting. She thinks of her grandmother's glove, mended and worn outward, and of forty pairs of hands that mended alongside her. The house is stationed. Julian is in the library with his unread book. Octavia is in the library with excellent hearing. Élise's village is watching the stranger's door. Harrow is at his keeping, with Élise's boy on the lane. And she is here, in the morning room, at eleven, being early on purpose. Punctuality, her grandmother used to say, is the first politeness and the last warning.)*

scenes.synopsis: dressing for the negotiation — archive silk, fashionable; the grandmother's pearls; the glove.
scenes.prose:
> *(Letitia lays out the deep teal silk, and Rose understands at once: this is not the grey of waiting. This is the archive at its most deliberate. The gown is twenty-five years old, cut in the high-waisted fashion of the century's turn, the bodice embroidered in gold thread that has gone soft but not dim. With it, the grandmother's pearls, the long rope, doubled. "If she is going to make you an offer," Letitia says, fastening the pearls, "she can make it to a woman dressed like the answer is no." Rose laughs, surprised. "Is that the doctrine?" "That's the doctrine," Letitia says, and means it.)*
> *(The mended gloves go on last. Pearl grey kid against deep teal, the mend at the thumb, the violet pinned at the wrist. In the glass, the whole argument of the negotiation: wealth without display, age without apology, the scar worn outward. "Fashionable," Rose says, studying the reflection. "Your grandmother," Letitia says, "never under-dressed an occasion out of literalism. Neither will you." She will wear the teal through the whole negotiation, the color of an answer not yet given, worn before the question is asked.)*

scenes.synopsis: Octavia's early counsel — hear everything, promise nothing; the messenger is furniture.
scenes.prose:
> *(Octavia arrives at half past eleven, takes one look at the teal silk, and says, "Good. Terrifying, but good." She settles into the library's far chair with her embroidery, which she will not touch. "Now. Last counsel, and then I become furniture. She will be polite. The politeness is the weapon. She will name a sum that sounds large until you divide it by what she's buying. She will give you a date, and the date will sound like a courtesy. It isn't. It's a lever." She looks up. "Ask her anything. Tell her nothing. And when she threatens —" "She'll threaten politely," Rose says. "That's the worst kind," Octavia agrees. "Rudeness you can answer. Politeness you can only out-wait.")*
> *("What if the sum is large?" Rose asks. "It will be large. Two thousand, I'd guess. Maybe three. It's large the way a bribe is large: exactly enough to make refusing it feel theatrical." Octavia sets the embroidery down. "Don't be theatrical. Be" — she gestures at the teal, the pearls, the glove — "be that. Interested. Unhurried. Faintly amused. Let her do the hurrying." Rose nods. The counsel, taken. "And Octavia," "Yes?" "Thank you. For the furniture." Octavia picks up the embroidery she won't touch. "It's the best seat in the house," she says.)*

scenes.synopsis: the quartermaster's arrangements — the room, the tea, the exits; everything, considered.
scenes.prose:
> *(Letitia's final check is military. "The good tea in the good pot. The biscuits she won't eat. You," she says, pointing at Rose, "in the chair facing the door, so she comes to you. Me, bringing the tray at half past, on a pretext, so I can see her face." She pauses. "Julian and Octavia in the library. The door between" — she indicates the morning room's inner door — "ajar. Not open. Ajar." Rose raises an eyebrow. "Ajar is not listening at doors." "Ajar," Letitia says firmly, "is ventilation.")*
> *("And if she offers money, you hear the sum. If she threatens, you offer more tea. If she cries . . ." A beat. "She won't cry." "How do you know?" "Women who cry for a living don't get sent to negotiate. They get sent to—" Letitia stops, reconsidering. "She won't cry." Rose looks at her quartermaster: the arrangements, the pretexts, the ajar door that is ventilation. "You're enjoying this," she says. "I'm good at it," Letitia says, which is not a denial.)*

scenes.synopsis: noon — Mrs. Quick arrives; the woman, seen plainly; the terms, about to be stated.
scenes.prose:
> *(The knocker sounds at noon exactly, and Letitia brings her in. The woman from the card is exactly as the card promised: plain, forty-five, dark gown, a reticule that looks like it carries documents. She curtsies correctly. "Miss Hartwell. Thank you for receiving me. I act for interested parties." She sits where she's shown, places the reticule on her lap, and folds her hands over it. The composure is total. It is also, Rose notes, professional: this is a woman who has sat in a hundred morning rooms and said difficult things in them.)*
> *("I will be brief," Mrs. Quick says, "because my instructions are precise, and precision respects your time." She opens the reticule and takes out a single folded paper, which she does not unfold. "There is a story about to be printed. Concerning your family's affairs during the late war. Concerning certain papers, and certain sums, and certain French names." She looks up. The eyes are grey and direct. "I am here to offer you the chance to sell it first. The papers, the story, the exclusive. Before Saturday." The room is very quiet. The good tea steams, untouched. The offer is in the room, stated the way Octavia predicted: politely, precisely, like a courtesy.)*

scenes.synopsis: the sum, named — two thousand pounds; the papers, the story, the exclusive; what the money buys.
scenes.prose:
> *("Two thousand pounds," Mrs. Quick says. She names it the way a clerk names a total: without emphasis, which is itself the emphasis. "For the papers in your possession, and the papers in Mr. Harrow's possession. For the exclusive right to the history they contain. For your" — the smallest pause — "cooperation in its telling." Rose does the arithmetic Octavia taught her: two thousand, divided by what they're buying. The sin, whole. The family's name, laundered through a purchased telling. Harrow's silence, bought with his own papers. The numbers are insulting. The politeness makes them more so.)*
> *("And if I decline?" Rose asks. She keeps her voice level, interested, faintly amused. The grandmother's face, worn like the teal. Mrs. Quick refolds nothing; nothing was unfolded. "Then the story will be printed without you," she says. "Mr. Pounce's paper, Saturday. Our version." The smallest emphasis on "our." "I should be candid, Miss Hartwell: our version will not flatter. It will, however, be first." She says it without malice. That is the worst of it. There is no malice to answer. There is only the transaction, stated politely, the way a woman states the price of a horse she intends to buy whether or not you sell.)*

scenes.synopsis: Rose's questions — every question worth asking; the principal, unnamed; the timetable, probed.
scenes.prose:
> *("May I ask questions?" Rose says. "Of course," Mrs. Quick says. "Though I should warn you, my instructions limit what I can answer." "Then I'll ask, and you'll tell me where the limits are." Rose settles back, the teal silk arranging itself. "Who are the interested parties?" "I am not instructed to say." "Is Mrs. Vane among them?" The smallest flicker. Not in the eyes; lower, at the mouth. "I am not instructed to say." "What does 'our version' contain that the papers don't?" "Interpretation," Mrs. Quick says smoothly. "The papers are" — she chooses the word — "incomplete. Our version completes them." "With invention?" "With context." The euphemism sits between them like the good tea, steaming and untouched.)*
> *("And Saturday," Rose says. "Is the date flexible?" "The date is set," Mrs. Quick says. "The type, I understand, is largely set as well." "Then why are you here Thursday?" The question lands. Mrs. Quick considers it, and for the first time the professionalism shows a seam. "Because," she says carefully, "my principal prefers a transaction to a . . ." She looks for the word. "To an event. Transactions can be managed. Events," she glances at the window, at Hartwell's park beyond it, "events have a way of exceeding their instructions." Rose nods slowly. The principal, unnamed, has told the truth once: she is afraid of what Rose will do. That is worth more than the two thousand.)*

scenes.synopsis: the threat, restated politely — Saturday's Lash, "our version"; Rose understands it perfectly.
scenes.prose:
> *("Let me be sure I understand," Rose says. She leans forward slightly, the pearls shifting. "You are offering me two thousand pounds for my family's papers, and for my cooperation in a telling managed by your principal. If I decline, Mr. Pounce prints his version on Saturday. A version you describe as unflattering, incomplete without your context, and first." Mrs. Quick inclines her head. "That is the offer." "And the papers in Mr. Harrow's possession —" "Are included in the price." "Mr. Harrow's cooperation?" "Would be," the smallest hesitation, "appreciated. Arranged separately, if necessary." The threat to Harrow, stated as an administrative detail. The room's temperature drops several degrees, though the tea still steams.)*
> *("I understand the offer perfectly," Rose says, in the manner Octavia taught her: interested, unhurried, faintly amused. "You want to buy the sin before I decide what to do with it. You want my signature on your version of my family's shame, so that when the truth comes out, as truths do, it comes out wearing your clothes." Mrs. Quick's composure doesn't crack. It adjusts, the way a good clerk adjusts a ledger. "That is" — she starts. "A colorful way of putting it," Rose finishes. "Yes. I have a colorful family." The grandmother's face holds. The politeness holds. Underneath both, the understanding is complete: they are afraid of her choosing, and they have come to buy the choosing from her.)*

scenes.synopsis: the politeness as weapon — Quick's final pressure, applied gently; the room, held.
scenes.prose:
> *(Mrs. Quick tries once more, and the trying is masterful. "Miss Hartwell," she says, leaning forward, the reticule forgotten, "let me speak, for a moment, not as an agent." A pause. The room waits. "I have carried terms to a dozen houses. I have seen what Saturday's papers do to families who decline. The version printed is never the version deserved. It is longer than the truth and shorter than justice, and it stays in the libraries." She says it gently. The gentleness is the pressure. "Two thousand pounds is a large sum. It would" — she glances around the morning room, at the teal silk, the pearls — "it would do a great deal. And the telling would be managed. Kindly managed. You would not be exposed.")*
> *(Rose hears the offer underneath the offer: not just money, but management. Kindness, purchased. The shame, laundered. It is, she realizes, the most insulting thing anyone has said to her in the whole affair, precisely because it is said with such genuine gentleness. Mrs. Quick believes she is being kind. That is what makes her dangerous. "You are very persuasive," Rose says. "It is my profession," Mrs. Quick says, without pride. "I know," Rose says. "That's why I'm going to give you my answer in writing. So there's no" — she smiles, the grandmother's smile — "misunderstanding between professionals." The gentleness, outwaited. The pressure, held.)*

scenes.synopsis: the answer — no answer on their timetable; Rose refuses the clock, politely and finally.
scenes.prose:
> *("My answer," Rose says, "is that I don't answer on timetables." She says it plainly, setting the grandmother's face aside for the moment, because this sentence deserves her own face. "I understand your offer. I understand your Saturday. I understand that your principal would prefer a transaction to an event." She looks at Mrs. Quick directly. "Tell your principal this: the sin is not for sale. Not for two thousand pounds, not on a Thursday, not before Saturday. What I do with my family's papers is my family's business, and I will do it when I decide, in the manner I decide. That is not a refusal of your Thursday. It is a refusal of your clock.")*
> *(Mrs. Quick is silent a moment. Then she nods, once, and puts the folded paper back in the reticule. It was never unfolded. It will never be unfolded. "I will convey your answer," she says. "May I" — she hesitates, the first unscripted moment — "may I ask, as a matter of professional curiosity, when you will decide?" Rose smiles. "Before Saturday," she says. "But not because of Saturday." Mrs. Quick looks at her for a long moment, and something like respect crosses her face. "I see," she says. "My principal will be interested." She rises. The call is over, and the clock with it.)*

scenes.synopsis: after the call — the glove, noticed; the teal, kept; the woman, unbent.
scenes.prose:
> *(Alone in the morning room, Rose looks down at her hands. The mended glove. Mrs. Quick had noticed it; Rose had seen the grey eyes drop to the thumb, once, and dismiss it as poverty. Let the woman think what she likes. The mend is not poverty. The mend is the doctrine. She flexes the thumb, feeling the small scar of stitches, and thinks about the two thousand pounds, refused. It had sounded large until Octavia's arithmetic divided it. Now it sounds like what it was: the price of her signature on someone else's version of her family's shame. Cheap, at any price.)*
> *(She does not change out of the teal. The day isn't done, and the gown is doing its work: every room she enters, the household reads the color and understands. The negotiation, held. The answer, given. The clock, refused. Letitia finds her in the hall and looks her up and down. "Well?" "In writing," Rose says. "Tonight." Letitia nods, satisfied. "Keep the teal for dinner," she says. "The house should see it." She will wear the refused color through dinner, unbent, and let the household read it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the parting — Saturday, named; the last look; the door, closed politely.
scenes.prose:
> *(Letitia shows her out, and Rose walks with them to the hall, because courtesy is also a weapon and she intends to be fully armed. At the door Mrs. Quick turns. "Saturday's Lash," she says quietly. "I wanted you to hear it from me, not from the village. The type is set. Whatever you decide before then —" she stops. The sentence doesn't finish, because finishing it would be negotiating, and the negotiation is over. "Thank you for the tea," she says instead. "It was very good tea." "It was the good tea," Rose says. "We knew the occasion." The smallest smile, shared between professionals.)*
> *(The carriage pulls away down the drive: plain, hired, no crest. Rose stands in the doorway and watches it go, the teal silk bright in the noon sun, the mended glove raised in the smallest farewell. Then she turns back into the house, and the household is there: Letitia in the hall, Octavia in the library doorway, Julian with his book upside down. "Well?" Octavia says. "She offered two thousand," Rose says, "for the sin, the story, and the exclusive. I told her the sin isn't for sale and I don't answer on timetables." A beat. Then Octavia says, "The teal was the right choice," and everyone laughs, and the tension of the morning breaks like a wave.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — THE ANSWER'S SHAPE: cold refusal, open door, or counter-question; the refusal, written.
scenes.prose:
> *(Afternoon. The refusal must go in writing; Rose promised it, and professionals keep promises. But the shape of the written refusal is its own decision. Three shapes offer themselves. The cold refusal: a single page, formal, final. "The sin is not for sale." No warmth, no explanation, no crack for a counter-offer to enter. The open door: a refusal of the price, not of the dealing. "Not for two thousand, not on a Thursday." It leaves the principal wondering what Thursday's refusal might become on Friday, which is a kind of leverage. The counter-question: answer the offer with a question of her own. "Who is Mrs. Vane, and what does she want with my family's shame?" It tells them she knows the name, which tells them their money has a face, which changes the negotiation's temperature without changing its terms.)*
> *(She takes up her pen and thinks of Mrs. Quick's grey eyes, of the respect that crossed them, of the woman who believed she was being kind. The written refusal will be read by the principal, whoever she is, and the principal will read it the way Rose read the blind item: for what it says, what it withholds, what it wants. She dips the pen. The shape, chosen, becomes the letter.)*
> *(She wrote the refusal in the shape she'd chosen, sealed it, and set it aside for the dawn post. Whatever the principal read in it — the shut door, the unclosed dealing, or the spoken name — it would be Rose's reading, not theirs. The letter was hers. The clock stayed hers.)*

options.label: Cold refusal
options.detail: *Resolve+; the door, shut.* A single formal page: the sin is not for sale. *(The principal learns nothing; the refusal is absolute, and absolutely uninformative.)*

options.label: Open door
options.detail: *Cunning+; the price, refused.* Not for two thousand, not on a Thursday; the dealing, unclosed. *(The principal wonders about Friday; the wondering is leverage.)*

options.label: Counter-question
options.detail: *Nerve+; the name, spoken.* Who is Mrs. Vane, and what does she want? *(The principal learns her money has a face; the temperature changes, the terms don't.)*

scenes.synopsis: the debrief — the offer was real; the money is real; the fear is real.
scenes.prose:
> *(Octavia's debrief is thorough. "Two thousand," she says. "Real money. Not a feint. And Saturday's type, set. Also real." She paces the library, the embroidery abandoned. "Here's what matters: she came. A principal who was only bluffing wouldn't send a woman like that on a Thursday. Mrs. Quick is expensive. You don't hire her to carry an empty threat." She stops. "They're afraid of you choosing. Quick as much as said it. 'Events exceed their instructions.'" Octavia looks at Rose. "You have something they want. Not the papers. The choosing. They want to buy it before you use it.")*
> *("Then the choosing is the weapon," Rose says slowly. "It's the only weapon," Octavia says. "Think: if you expose, their version dies. If you bury, their version starves. If you atone . . ." She stops. "If I atone, their version is irrelevant," Rose finishes. "A debt confessed can't be blackmailed." Octavia nods. "That's the door I haven't priced yet. But know this: whatever it costs, it's the one they can't touch. The other two doors, they can at least describe. The third," she smiles, thin, "the third door doesn't have their fingerprints on it at all." The debrief, done. The weapon, identified: the choosing itself.)*

scenes.synopsis: Bell on the law — what Pounce can print Saturday; libel, truth, and the space between.
scenes.prose:
> *(Bell comes at three with the law in her pocket, or as much of it as Grub Street respects. "He can print what he can defend," she says bluntly. "Truth is a defense. Opinion is a defense. 'We hear' is not a defense, but it's cheap to print and expensive to sue, which is why Pounce lives in the gap." She ticks the Saturday possibilities on her fingers. "One: he prints the blind item again, louder. Two: he prints names. De Varennes. Sums. If he's bought the details somewhere, he prints them. Three: he prints lies, and dares you to sue." She looks at Rose. "Lies are the likeliest. Lies are cheap, and the truth is still in your drawer.")*
> *("And if he prints lies?" "Then you sue, and the suit takes a year, and the year takes the story with it. Or" — Bell leans forward — "you print the truth first, and the lies die of irrelevance. That's the only libel action that works in a week." She stands. "My offer stands, Miss Hartwell. The true account, whole and untrimmed. My press, your story, nobody's money. When you're ready." She goes, leaving the law on the table. Rose sits with it: the gap Pounce lives in, the year a suit takes, the week the truth needs.)*

scenes.synopsis: Harrow, told of the offer — the witness hears the price on his papers; his steadiness, confirmed.
scenes.prose:
> *(She rides to the village at four, because Harrow heard about the call before she arrived; the village's telegraph is faster than horses. He is at his table, the cloth over the papers, and he looks up with the question already in his face. "Two thousand," Rose says, before he asks. "For both halves. And your cooperation, arranged separately." Harrow is quiet a long moment. Then: "That's less than my mother's house sold for." The dryness, intact. "They priced the sin at less than a house." "They priced your signature," Rose corrects. "The sin they were going to take anyway. Saturday." She tells him about Mrs. Quick, the politeness, the timetable refused.)*
> *(He listens completely, without moving, and then he does the thing she has come to count on: he steadies. "You refused the clock," he says. "Good. Clocks are how they hurry people into bad decisions." He touches the cloth over his papers. "My half stays mine until you decide, Miss Hartwell. Whatever door you take" — he stops, because they haven't named the doors, not yet — "whatever you decide, the papers go with your decision. Not before." Rose looks at him: the witness, the keeper of the other half, offering the only thing he has. "Thank you," she says. It is inadequate, and he knows it, and accepts it anyway.)*

scenes.synopsis: the glove, given — Rose gives Harrow her grandmother's spare; the witness, mended in.
scenes.prose:
> *(It happens as she's leaving. She looks at his hands on the table, bare, ink-stained, the hands that carried the papers for twenty years, and she thinks of the mending table, the forty pairs, the household's uniform. "Wait," she says. She takes off her right glove, the spare from the drawer that morning, pearl grey, mended at the thumb by her grandmother's own hand. "For the witness," she says, and holds it out. Harrow stares at it. "Miss Hartwell, I —" "It's a glove, Mr. Harrow. Not a commission." He takes it slowly, as if it might be hot. It fits. Of course it fits; the afternoon seems arranged to make it fit.)*
> *("I don't —" he starts. "Mend things?" Rose finishes. "You will. There's a table in the servants' hall. Letitia will show you." He looks at the glove on his hand, the mend at the thumb, and something in his face does the thing faces do when they stop being alone. "Forty pairs," he says quietly. "Forty," Rose agrees, "and the forty-first glove." She rides home in the dusk with one glove on and one glove given away, and the asymmetry feels exactly right: the witness, mended in. The household, forty — and one.)*

scenes.synopsis: Laurent, held — the fury at the offer; the émigré's son, kept from the lane.
scenes.prose:
> *(Laurent is waiting when she returns, and the black coat is still on, and the fury has a new object. "Two thousand," he says. Élise told him. "They priced it. They put a number on —" he can't finish. He doesn't need to. "Sit down," Rose says. He sits, which surprises them both. "They offered," she says, "and I refused the clock. That's the whole of it. The sum doesn't matter." "The sum matters," Laurent says. "It's what they think we're worth." "It's what they think I'm worth frightened," Rose corrects. "There's a difference." He looks at her, the teal silk, the single glove, the calm. "You're not frightened." "I'm furious," Rose says. "I'm just better dressed.")*
> *(He laughs, startled, the fury cracking. "Your grandmother's doctrine." "Stitch by stitch." They sit a moment in the hall, the émigré's son and the sinner's granddaughter, and the fury settles into something harder and more useful: resolve. "Saturday," Laurent says. "If they print —" "When they print," Rose corrects. "Something. Then we act. Not before." He nods slowly. "I can wait until Saturday." "Can you?" "I can wait until Saturday," he repeats, firmer. "After Saturday, I make no promises." It is the most honest thing anyone has said all day. Rose accepts it as the promise it is.)*

scenes.synopsis: Julian's other offer — to buy the sheet; the suitor's money, weighed and declined.
scenes.prose:
> *(Julian finds her in the library at six, and he doesn't waste time. "Let me buy it," he says. "The Lash. Pounce, the press, the whole squalid enterprise. I've had Quill look into it. Twelve hundred pounds would do it. The paper stops Saturday, the type is melted, Pounce retires to the country." He says it the way he used to offer his sword: eagerly, completely, as if money solved things. Rose looks at him in the teal silk, the pearls, the single glove, and feels the old Brighton fury rise in him, barely leashed. "And then?" she says.)*
> *("And then it's done." "And then I've bought a newspaper to suppress a story," Rose says. "Which is a story. Which Pounce's successor prints." She takes his hand. "Julian. It's a generous offer. It's also the wrong weapon. If I buy the sheet, I'm the woman who bought the press. If I print the truth, I'm the woman who told it. There's a difference." He looks at her a long moment, the eagerness draining, the steadiness returning. "The teal," he says at last. "You wore the teal, and I offered to buy a newspaper. I see the disproportion." "Next to," Rose says. "Not in front." "Next to," he agrees. The offer, declined. The suitor, steady.)*

fashionChoices.label: Decline, warmly
fashionChoices.detail: the generosity honored; the weapon, refused.

fashionChoices.label: Decline, coldly
fashionChoices.detail: the lesson, repeated; Brighton, recalled.

fashionChoices.label: Hold it in reserve
fashionChoices.detail: not now; perhaps never; the option, kept.

scenes.synopsis: the arithmetic of refusal — two thousand pounds, weighed against the sin; the sum, dismissed.
scenes.prose:
> *(Alone at dusk, Rose does the arithmetic properly. Two thousand pounds. Against it: the papers, both halves. The de Varennes' ruin. The de Valcourts' losses. Harrow's twenty years. Her grandfather's name. Her own name. The household's forty pairs of mended gloves. Élise's violets. The wall, the breach, the spring. She writes the two sums on a scrap of paper, the way her grandmother taught her: what they offer, what it costs. The second column runs off the page. The first column sits there, small and precise and insulting. Two thousand pounds. Less than Harrow's mother's house.)*
> *(She folds the scrap and puts it in the drawer with the Lash and Bell's draft: the probe, the answer, and now the price, filed together. The arithmetic of refusal, complete. It was never about the money. It was about the signature: they wanted her to sign their version, to launder the sin through her cooperation, to make the telling manageable. Kindly managed. She looks at her single glove, the mend at the thumb. Some things can't be managed. Some things can only be mended, or told, or paid for. Saturday will bring their version. She will bring hers. The sums, dismissed. The signature, withheld.)*

scenes.synopsis: the stranger's movements — the village watch reports; the hunter, restless.
scenes.prose:
> *(Élise's evening report is short and interesting. "He's restless," she says. "The Crown's boy says he paced the yard this morning. He walked to Harrow's keeping at noon, stood off it for ten minutes, and walked back. He asked the carrier, again, about parcels." She sets down a posy of violets. "And there's this: a letter came for him at the Crown. By the afternoon post. He read it in the yard, and the boy says his face" — she pauses — "the boy says he looked like a man whose instructions changed." Rose picks up a violet. "Mrs. Quick's report," she says. "Telling him the Thursday call failed.")*
> *("He'll press harder now," Élise says. "Or he'll wait for Saturday." "He'll press," Rose says. She knows the type: the timetable man, the instructions changed, the principal displeased. "Double the watch on Harrow's keeping. And Élise" — she holds the violet, faithfulness — "thank your neighborhood for me. The blacksmith's haunting. Mrs. Pike's girl's French poetry. Tell them the mistress laughed." Élise smiles, the flower-seller's smile that has become a spymaster's. "They'll like that," she says. "The village likes being in on the joke." The watch, doubled. The hunter, restless.)*

scenes.synopsis: Augusta, before dinner — the name, kept out; the boundary, reaffirmed lightly.
scenes.prose:
> *(Augusta finds her in the hall before dinner, and the conversation is brief, which is how Augusta prefers everything. "The caller," she says. "Gone?" "Gone," Rose says. "And?" "Two thousand. Refused." Augusta nods, once. "Good." A pause. Then, carefully: "The de Valcourt name. In whatever comes." "Stays out," Rose says. "My word holds." Augusta studies her: the teal silk, the single glove, the woman who refused two thousand pounds before lunch. "You look," she says, "like someone who has stopped asking permission." "I stopped," Rose says, "some time ago." The smallest smile, shared. Not warmth, exactly. Alliance.)*
> *(As Augusta turns to go, she adds, over her shoulder: "Your grandmother wore that teal to a rout in '89. The French ambassador's wife asked where it was made. Your grandmother said, 'In my wardrobe, madame, twenty years ago.' The woman never recovered." Rose laughs, delighted. "Did she really?" "She embroidered the story a little," Augusta admits. "But the teal is real. Wear it well." The kinship, light. The boundary, firm. The teal, twenty-five years old, doing its work.)*

scenes.synopsis: the law, again — what Saturday prints and what Monday sues; the solicitor's counsel, practical.
scenes.prose:
> *(Quill dines with them, and over the fish he gives the legal position the way other men give the weather. "Saturday he prints. Monday you could sue. The suit takes a year. In the year, the story lives in every library in England." He lays down his fork. "Or: Saturday he prints, and Saturday afternoon the Gazette prints the truth, and by Monday Pounce is old news." He looks at Rose. "Bell's right. The only libel action that works in a week is the truth, printed first." Laurent, down the table, says, "Or we —" "We don't," Quill says, without looking up. "Whatever you're about to suggest, we don't. The law is slow, but it's the only weapon that doesn't become the story.")*
> *(Rose considers the fish, the law, and the week. "So the choices are: sue and wait, or print and pre-empt." "Or," Quill says, "the third thing nobody's pricing yet." He glances at Octavia, who glances at her plate. The atonement door, unpriced, sits at the dinner table like an uninvited guest everyone can see. "We'll price it," Rose says quietly. "Soon." Octavia nods. The fish is removed. The law, stated. The third thing, waiting.)*

scenes.synopsis: the grandfather's desk — heirlooms inventoried; what can be sold and what can't.
scenes.prose:
> *(After dinner she goes to the study, to her grandfather's desk. Not the papers; the drawers. The heirlooms, inventoried the way Quill inventoried the paper: the seal ring, the watch, the miniature of her grandmother as a girl, the silver inkstand. She handles each one, weighing not the value but the keepability. The seal ring: keep. The watch: keep. The miniature: keep, obviously. The inkstand: sellable, but — she sets it down. Everything here is sellable. Nothing here is for sale. That is the difference between an heirloom and an asset, and her grandfather, for all his sins, understood it: he played with other people's money, never with the plate.)*
> *(She finds, in the desk's deep drawer, a pair of gloves. Men's. Mended at the thumb, in a hand she recognizes: her grandmother's stitching, on her grandfather's glove. She sits with them a long moment. He kept them. The man who played wartime funds with émigré money kept his wife's mended gloves in his desk's deep drawer. People are never one thing. That is the hardest lesson of the season, and the desk teaches it without a word. She puts the gloves back, closes the drawer. The heirlooms, inventoried. The man, uninventoried.)*

fashionChoices.label: Keep everything
fashionChoices.detail: the archive, intact; nothing sold, whatever comes.

fashionChoices.label: Price the sellable
fashionChoices.detail: know the values, in case the restitution needs them.

fashionChoices.label: Give the gloves to Harrow
fashionChoices.detail: the grandfather's mended pair, to the witness.

scenes.synopsis: Letitia's vow — she will not be silent again; the quartermaster, as witness.
scenes.prose:
> *(Letitia comes to the study at nine, and she doesn't sit. "I need to say something," she says, "and I need you not to manage me while I say it." Rose closes the desk drawer. "Say it." "When this" — Letitia gestures at the desk, the house, the season — "when this comes out, as it will, in whatever manner you choose, I want to be on record. I knew the shape. I kept silent. I am not proud of the silence. If there's a telling, I want my silence in it. Not hidden. Not managed.")*
> *("It will be in it," Rose says quietly. "Whatever door I take, Letitia. The expose tells everything. The bury" — she stops, because they both know the bury tells nothing — "the atone tells what matters. Your silence will be in it. Not as shame. As the shape of the household. The way we kept things then. The way we don't, now." Letitia nods, once. "Then I'm ready," she says. "For whichever." She goes. The vow, made. The witness, volunteered.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — THE PAPERS' KEEPING: Hartwell's strongbox, Harrow's cottage, or Quill's keeping; the halves, placed.
scenes.prose:
> *(Night. The question of the papers won't wait for Saturday: two halves, two places, and a hunter who wants them both. Three keepings offer themselves. Bring both halves to Hartwell: the strongbox, the iron, the oak, the household's guard. Safe behind the gates. But together, which means one fire, one theft, one disaster takes everything, and a house holding both halves looks like a house hiding something. Leave Harrow's half in his keeping: divided, as now. The village's guard, the misinformation, the ordinary. But the stranger is watching his keeping, and Saturday's pressure will fall on Harrow first. Lodge copies with Quill: the solicitor's keeping, the law's roof. Neither house nor cottage, but the third place, neutral and documented. Copies, not originals; the originals stay divided. The lawyer's answer. The one that trusts the system.)*
> *(Rose rides to his keeping in the dark; Harrow is awake, the lamp lit, the cloth over his papers. She puts it to him plainly. He listens, and then he says the thing that decides it: "My half has lived here three years, Miss Hartwell. It's safer here than anywhere, because here it's" — he looks around the one good room — "here it's just papers. At Hartwell it would be evidence. At Quill's it would be a file." She looks at him, the steady hands, the single mended glove on his right hand. And chooses.)*
> *(She placed the papers the way she'd place anything she meant to keep: deliberately, and apart from each other. Harrow nodded at the placing, the lamp lit, the cloth undisturbed. Whatever Saturday brought, the halves would meet it from two addresses.)*

options.label: Both halves at Hartwell
options.detail: *Resolve+; the strongbox, filled.* Iron, oak, the household's guard; one roof, one risk. *(Safe behind gates; London reads the gathering as hiding.)*

options.label: Divided, as now
options.detail: *Composure+; the halves, separated.* His keeping, her strongbox; no single fire takes all. *(Harrow bears Saturday's pressure; the village bears it with him.)*

options.label: Copies with Quill
options.detail: *Prudence+; the law's roof.* The solicitor's keeping; documented, neutral, third-placed. *(The system trusted; the originals stay divided and unfiled.)*

scenes.synopsis: evening, the cost of "their version" — what Saturday's lies would do to the innocent; the stakes, named.
scenes.prose:
> *(Octavia stays the night, and over the bedroom fire she names the thing nobody's named: what Pounce's version does to people who aren't Rose. "Harrow," she says, counting on her fingers. "Sixty-one, the village's own, becomes 'the accomplice' in every library in England. Letitia becomes 'the silent servant.' The de Varennes" — she stops — "the de Varennes become a paragraph. Their ruin, a paragraph, in a gutter sheet, read over breakfast and forgotten by lunch." She looks at Rose. "Your grandfather becomes a villain, which he wasn't, quite. He was weaker than that. Villains are simple. He was complicated, which is worse for everyone.")*
> *("So their version hurts the innocent and simplifies the guilty," Rose says. "That's what gutter sheets do," Octavia says. "It's the business model." They sit with the fire a moment. Then Octavia says, quietly: "This is why the third door matters, Rose. Expose tells the truth, but the truth still has Harrow as 'the accomplice' for a week. Bury hides everyone, including the guilty, which isn't justice. Atone" — she stops — "atone pays Harrow. Names the de Varennes as creditors, not victims. It's the only door where the innocent get something." She doesn't name the price. Not yet. "Soon," Rose says. "Soon," Octavia agrees. The stakes, named. The innocent, counted.)*

scenes.synopsis: dinner in the teal — the household sees the color of the refused; archive dress, at estate scale.
scenes.prose:
> *(She keeps the teal for dinner, as Letitia advised, and the household reads it at once: the negotiation held, the answer given, the clock refused. The dining room is archive dress at estate scale. Laurent in his father's black coat. Octavia in grey silk that predates the century. Augusta in dark blue velvet, twenty years old, perfect. Letitia in her best black, the quartermaster's uniform. The mended gloves, forty pairs, at every place. The violets, at every wrist. It looks less like dinner and more like a court: the court of the unflinching, convened in teal and black and grey.)*
> *(The talk is ordinary, deliberately: the wall's third course, the canal's levels, the puppy's crimes. But underneath the ordinary runs the day's current — the offer refused, Saturday coming, the choosing nearer. Rose looks down the table at her people, the teal silk bright among them, and feels what she felt at the mending table: not strategy, but the loyalty underneath it. Her household. Her forty. Whatever Saturday prints, it prints about people who mended gloves together. That is not nothing. That, she thinks, is nearly everything.)*

fashionChoices.label: Teal through the evening
fashionChoices.detail: the color, worn till bedtime; the statement, sustained.

fashionChoices.label: The pearls, kept on
fashionChoices.detail: the heirloom, through dessert; continuity, displayed.

fashionChoices.label: Letitia's reading
fashionChoices.detail: the quartermaster judges the room.

scenes.synopsis: the lane, watched — the stranger's evening move; the hunter, closer.
scenes.prose:
> *(Élise's boy runs in during dessert with the evening's news: the stranger has left the Crown. He's on the lane to Harrow's keeping, walking fast, no longer strolling. Élise is already pulling on her shawl. "The churchyard," she says. "I'll see what he does." Rose stands. "No," she says. "We —" She stops. The table is watching: Laurent half out of his chair, Julian setting down his glass, Octavia very still. "Élise goes," Rose says quietly. "It's her watch. But Julian goes with her. And Laurent," she looks at him, "stays here. That's the order." Laurent sits, slowly. The fury, leashed. For now.)*
> *(They wait through the pudding. The dining room's ordinary talk doesn't resume; nobody pretends. Then Élise returns, Julian behind her, and her report is short. "He knocked," she says. "Harrow didn't answer. He knocked again. Then he left a letter at the door and walked back to the village." A letter. At Harrow's door. The table exhales, collectively. "And Harrow?" Rose asks. "Harrow," Élise says, "watched from the window, the way you taught the village to watch. He hasn't touched the letter. He's waiting for you." Rose nods. The hunter, closer. The witness, steady.)*

scenes.synopsis: the archive ritual — the grandfather's strongbox opened; heirlooms handled; the papers laid beside the plate; the chapter's ritual.
scenes.prose:
> *(System: commit to a direction, A, B, or C, then twenty 5-coin pins. 20 pins × 5 coins = 100 coins. Re-picks always free; the jewel shelf stays open and is never a ritual step.)*
> *(Story morsel: Letitia, at the strongbox — "your grandmother opened this twice a year. Spring and Michaelmas. Like a reckoning.")*
> *(Story morsel: Octavia, watching — "dress the reckoning, Rose. The papers respect a woman who doesn't under-dress them.")*
> *(Story morsel: Harrow, at the door — "I never saw the strongbox. Twenty years, and I never saw inside.")*
> *(Story morsel: Rose, at the lamp — "Saturday they print their version. Whatever I do, I do knowing the whole of the archive.")*
> *(Story morsel: Letitia, at the door — "whatever you decide, miss. The archive stands behind you.")*

ritual.occasionBrief: The offer has been refused and the clock with it. Saturday's type is set. Before the choosing, the archive: the grandfather's strongbox opened, the heirlooms handled, the papers laid beside the plate. Dress for the reckoning: the archive's finest, fashionable and deliberate, the grandmother's doctrine in every thread. Precise. Deliberate. Unafraid. The house that knows its archive does not flinch from it.

scenes.synopsis: the violet on the papers — faithfulness, laid on the sin; the quiet, after the reckoning.
scenes.prose:
> *(After the ritual she sits a moment in the study, the strongbox closed, the lamp low. Élise's violet lies on the desk where she left it, and Rose picks it up and holds it to the light. Faithfulness. The season's flower, the household's emblem, forty wrists — and the forty-first glove. She thinks about what faithfulness means, applied to the sin: not loyalty to the grandfather, who doesn't deserve it. Loyalty to the people the sin touched. Harrow, with his one glove. The de Varennes, a paragraph in a gutter sheet. Letitia, with her unproud silence. Faithfulness, she decides, is not keeping the secret. It's keeping the people.)*
> *(She lays the violet on the strongbox lid, a small purple fact against the iron. Then she blows out the lamp and goes up to bed, the teal silk exchanged for the nightdress, the pearls coiled, the single glove set out for morning. The house is quiet. The watch is out. Saturday is coming with its set type. And she, the woman who refused two thousand pounds before lunch, sleeps the sleep of the decided, or near enough to it that the difference doesn't matter.)*

scenes.synopsis: the timetable's legality — what Thursday's refusal changes; the solicitor's reading, dry.
scenes.prose:
> *(Quill walks her to the stables at dawn, because Quill does his best thinking around horses. "Your refusal," he says, "changes nothing legally and everything practically. Legally, Pounce can still print Saturday. Practically, you've told his principal that the transaction is off, which means the principal's money is now spent on a story, not a purchase." He offers the mare a carrot. "Money spent on stories is money that wants a return. They'll want it bigger, louder, sooner. Saturday's version will be enthusiastic.")*
> *("Enthusiastic," Rose repeats. "That's one word for libel." "It's the word their solicitor will use," Quill says. "If they have one. Which" — he feeds the mare — "I doubt." They walk a moment in the stable's good smell, leather and hay and the morning. "One more thing," Quill says. "Your letter. The shape you chose. It'll be read in London by people who read letters for a living. Whatever shape it is, it'll teach them something." "Then let it teach the right thing," Rose says. The timetable, parsed. The law, dry. The morning, good.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — THE TIMETABLE: answer before Saturday, let Saturday come, or pre-empt; the clock, met on her terms.
scenes.prose:
> *(Dawn. The refusal is sealed for the post. Saturday's Lash is set in type. Between them, forty-eight hours, and the question of how to spend them. Three spendings offer themselves. Answer before Saturday: decide now, act Friday, meet their date with her own event. The pre-emption, early. It steals their Saturday by arriving first, but it hurries the choosing, and hurried choosing is what the whole week has refused. Let Saturday come: do nothing until the issue is in her hands. Read their version, then answer it. The discipline of the unhurried, carried to its limit. It risks letting the lie settle for a day. Pre-empt sideways: don't answer the story, answer around it. Set Bell's press, ready Quill, warn the village, prepare each door without choosing. The readiness, complete. Saturday arrives to find Hartwell already standing wherever it lands.)*
> *(She stands at the stable door with the mare breathing warm against her shoulder, and thinks of Mrs. Quick's grey eyes, of the stranger's letter at Harrow's door, of the type sitting in Pounce's galleys. The timetable was theirs. The spending of it is hers. She chooses how the forty-eight hours go.)*
> *(Forty-eight hours, spent her way: in action, in stillness, or in readiness. The stable door closed behind her. The mare went back to her hay. And the timetable, which had been theirs on Thursday, became hers by Friday.)*

options.label: Answer before Saturday
options.detail: *Resolve+; the pre-emption, early.* Decide now, act Friday; meet their date with her own event. *(Their Saturday is stolen; the choosing is hurried, against the week's doctrine.)*

options.label: Let Saturday come
options.detail: *Composure+; the unhurried, complete.* Do nothing till the issue is in hand; read it, then answer. *(The lie settles for a day; the answer lands on read ground.)*

options.label: Pre-empt sideways
options.detail: *Prudence+; the readiness, total.* Set the press, ready Quill, warn the village; prepare each door unchosen. *(Saturday finds Hartwell standing wherever it lands; nothing is hurried, everything is ready.)*

scenes.synopsis: the decision's first consequence — the household, told or untold; the orders, adjusted.
scenes.prose:
> *(She tells Letitia first, because the quartermaster needs to know how the forty-eight hours go. Letitia listens, nods, and adjusts the siege orders with a pencil: the watch doubled on his keeping, the gates locked at dusk, the good tea kept ready. "And Saturday?" she asks. "Saturday we read," Rose says. "Whatever the hours hold." Letitia makes the note. "The household can stand forty-eight hours," she says. "We've stood longer." She looks up. "Anything else?" "Yes," Rose says. "Tell the mending table: Saturday's gloves get an extra stitch. For luck." Letitia writes it down without smiling, which means she's smiling inside.)*
> *(The orders go up. The household reads them and understands: the mistress has a plan, the plan has a shape, the shape is hers. That is all the household needs. Rose watches from the hall as the servants disperse to their posts, the mended gloves on every hand, the violets at every wrist, and feels the campaign-calm settle for the second day running. Whatever the forty-eight hours bring, the house will meet them mended. The consequence, enacted. The orders, standing.)*

scenes.synopsis: the sting — Bell's draft: "The Offer, Declined"; the weapon, aimed at Saturday.
scenes.prose:
> *(The sting arrives with the noon post, in Bell's own hand, marked for Rose's eyes: the proprietor's new draft, and the headline set in type: "THE OFFER, DECLINED — On Two Thousand Pounds and a Thursday." Three paragraphs, cool and level. They describe, without naming, a lady who called at noon with terms; a sum named for papers and cooperation; a timetable refused. The last line is the aim: "The Gazette notes that some stories are bought. This paper has not bought this one. When it is told, it will be told because it is true. Saturday's readers may compare the two accounts, and judge which was purchased." Bell's rule holds: no names. But the warning is unmistakable, and it's aimed at Saturday.)*
> *(Rose reads it twice and understands the weapon's new shape: Bell has drafted the answer to Pounce's Saturday issue in advance, and the draft waits, as drafts do. "Saturday's readers may compare." The invitation, extended to the whole town. The hunters, told without being told: the Gazette is watching, and the Gazette cannot be bought. She files the draft with the Lash, the refusal's arithmetic, and the probe: the drawer is becoming an archive of the siege. The blade, aimed. Saturday, coming.)*
scenes.sting: THE OFFER, DECLINED — On Two Thousand Pounds and a Thursday.

scenes.synopsis: the refusal, written — the letter, composed in the chosen shape; the professionals' correspondence.
scenes.prose:
> *(She writes it at dusk, in the study, in the shape she chose. The pen moves the way it moves when the words are already decided: steadily. What she writes, the principal will know by Saturday's post: the cold page, the unclosed dealing, or the spoken name. Each shape is a different letter. Each letter is the same refusal. The sin is not for sale. The clock is not theirs. The choosing is not bought. She signs it with her full name, which she rarely does, because this letter is not from the granddaughter or the freeholder. It is from Rose Hartwell, plain, and it means what it says.)*
> *(She seals it with the plain band, no crest, and addresses it to Mrs. Quick, at the direction the card gave. The dawn post will carry it. By Saturday, the principal will have read it, and will know what Thursday taught: that the woman in the teal silk hears everything, promises nothing, and answers on no timetable but her own. She sets the sealed letter on the desk, beside Élise's violet. The refusal, written. The professionals' correspondence, complete.)*

scenes.synopsis: undressing — the teal, hung; the glove's mend, examined; the day, unpinned.
scenes.prose:
> *(The bedroom, late. The teal silk comes off and is hung with care; it has done its work and earned its rest. The pearls are coiled, the rope wound. The single glove — the left, the kept one — comes last. She holds it to the lamp the way she held its pair the night before: the grandmother's mend, the tiny stitches, even as print, holding. Mrs. Quick dismissed it as poverty. Mrs. Quick was wrong about several things. The mend held through a negotiation. It will hold through Saturday. It will hold through whatever comes after.)*
> *(She lays the glove beside tomorrow's violet and unpins her hair. The day unpins with it: the noon call, the two thousand, the grey eyes, the refused clock, the letter sealed for dawn. Each pin down. Each fact kept. She is tired the way a woman is tired after a day of being exactly herself. The lamp lowered. The teal, hung. The mend, holding. The day, done.)*

scenes.synopsis: the friends' talk — Octavia stays the night; what the offer cost and what it proved.
scenes.prose:
> *(At eleven Octavia comes to the bedroom, dressing-gowned, with two cups of chocolate. "Debrief," she says. "The unofficial one." They sit by the fire. "What did it cost?" Octavia asks. "The morning," Rose says. "And the illusion that they might be reasonable." Octavia nods. "And what did it prove?" "That they're afraid," Rose says. "Quick as much as said it. Events exceed instructions. They're afraid of what I'll do." "Good," Octavia says. "Fear is information. What will you do?" Rose looks into the chocolate. "Before Saturday," she says. "But not because of Saturday." Octavia smiles. "The teal was the right choice," she says. "I keep telling you. Nobody listens.")*
> *("Octavia." "Yes?" "The price. The atonement price. I'm ready." The fire crackles. Octavia is quiet a long moment. "Tomorrow," she says. "I'll bring my ledger. It's a lot of money, Rose. And it's not just money. It's the shape of the next ten years." "I know." "Do you?" "I'm starting to." Octavia nods slowly. "Tomorrow, then. The price, named. Precise and loving. I'll try for loving." "You don't have to try," Rose says. The friends' talk, done. The price, coming.)*

scenes.synopsis: the letter, dispatched — dawn; the post; the refusal, on its way.
scenes.prose:
> *(Dawn. She carries the sealed letter to the post herself, walking down the drive in the grey shawl with the mended glove in her pocket, because some errands shouldn't be delegated. The lodge keeper takes it, promises the morning post, and she walks back up the drive as the sun comes over the park wall. The letter is on its way. By Saturday, the principal will have read it. By Saturday, the stranger will have his new instructions. By Saturday, Pounce's type will roll. The forty-eight hours, begun.)*
> *(She stops at the breach in the walled garden, the wall half rebuilt, the gap still there. Soon the gap will close, stone by stone. Soon the papers will be whatever she decides. Exposed, buried, atoned. The three doors, still unnamed, stand in the morning mist like furniture she hasn't placed. She touches the wall's new stones, cool and solid. "Stitch by stitch," she says to the empty garden. The garden, half mended, seems to agree. The letter, dispatched. The hours, hers.)*

scenes.synopsis: the cliffhanger — the letter delivered; the stranger's new instructions; "Saturday, then."
scenes.prose:
> *(The Crown's yard, noon. The post comes, and the boy brings the letters, and the stranger takes his and reads it standing in the yard, the hired carriage of Thursday's caller long gone from the village. His face does nothing, then everything — the look of changed instructions. He folds the letter — Rose's refusal, in its chosen shape, the cold page or the open dealing or the spoken name — and puts it in his coat. Then he looks down the lane toward Harrow's keeping, and the look is the look of a man deciding whether to knock.)*
> *(He doesn't knock. Not yet. He turns back into the Crown and writes his own letter, quickly, the pen scratching. The village's telegraph will later report its direction: London. Its contents, no one knows. But that evening, Pounce's compositor is seen setting fresh type, and the tavern talk says Saturday's Lash will carry more than a blind item. The stranger stands at the Crown's window as the light fails, looking at the lane, looking at his keeping, looking at the big house on the hill. "Saturday, then," he says, to no one. The date, set. The screw, about to turn.)*

scenes.synopsis: Friday morning — Octavia is coming with her ledger; the day of accounting, begun.
scenes.prose:
> *(Friday morning comes up grey and businesslike, and Rose is glad of it. The week has been probes and offers and refused clocks. Today is numbers. Octavia arrives at ten with a leather ledger under her arm and the look of a woman carrying a sum. "It's done," she says, without preamble. "The counting. All of it." She sets the ledger on the morning room table the way a surgeon sets out instruments. "Before I open it," she says, "dress for it. This takes a while, and you'll want the pearls.")*
> *(Rose goes up and dresses for accounting: the dove grey silk, re-cut this spring, fashionable and severe; the grandmother's pearls, the long rope; the mended gloves. In the glass, the woman who will hear the price. She comes down, and Octavia looks her up and down and nods. "Good," she says. "Precise." She opens the ledger. The day of accounting, begun.)*

scenes.synopsis: the accounting dress — dove grey, re-cut; the pearls; precision, worn.
scenes.prose:
> *(Letitia fastens the pearls with unusual care. "Octavia's ledger," she says. "I've seen that look before. When she did the Harrington accounts." "And?" "And the Harringtons paid for ten years and thanked her." She steps back. "The grey," she says, "is the right choice. Numbers respect grey." Rose studies the glass: the dove silk, the re-cut bodice, the rope of pearls, the mended glove at the wrist. Fashionable, severe, precise. The woman who will hear the price looks like she can bear it.)*
> *("Whatever it is," Letitia says quietly, "the house stands it." "Whatever it is," Rose agrees. They go down together, the mistress and the quartermaster, to the morning room where the ledger waits. The accounting dress, complete. The pearls, precise. The woman, ready.)*

scenes.synopsis: the ledger, opened — Octavia's method; how she counted.
scenes.prose:
> *(Octavia opens the ledger, and the method is stated first. "I counted three debts," she says. "Harrow's wages, three years unpaid. The émigré principal, lost in your grandfather's play. The interest, because money owed accrues whether you acknowledge it or not." She turns the pages: Harrow's column, the de Varenne column, the de Valcourt column, each in her neat hand. "I used the estate's papers for the sums, Quill's counsel for the law, and my own judgment for the rest. The judgment is where the affection is. You'll see.")*
> *("Start with Harrow," Rose says. "I started with Harrow," Octavia says. She turns to his page. "Fifty pounds a year, for twenty years. One thousand pounds in wages — but he was paid for seventeen of them, in the village living, in clerk's fees, in Elias's guilt-guineas when the conscience bit. Three years stand unpaid." She writes the sum at the foot of the column: £150. "A hundred and fifty, paid at once. A man owed wages is a man lending his labor, and the labor's priced. Plus his keeping, deeded — a man of sixty-one should own his roof." The method, stated. The first debt, priced.)*

scenes.synopsis: the fortune, stated — what Hartwell holds; surplus, defined.
scenes.prose:
> *(Letitia is called in for the fortune, because the quartermaster knows the accounts better than the solicitor. "The fortune," she says, "stands thus. The Park, entailed, untouchable. The canal shares, paying three thousand a year. The London funds, nine thousand eight hundred in the surplus — that's above the household's needs, the estate's needs, and a prudent reserve." She looks at Octavia. "Nine thousand eight hundred, liquid. That's the now-money." Octavia nods, writing. "And the canal?" "Three thousand a year," Letitia says, "barring flood or folly. It's been three thousand for six years.")*
> *("So," Octavia says, "eight thousand eight hundred now from the surplus, keeping a thousand in reserve. Three thousand a year for ten years, from the canal." She writes the two figures. "Forty-one thousand six hundred, all told." Letitia looks at Rose. "The house stands it," she says again. "The roofs stay. The stones stay. The household's bread is not in it." The fortune, stated. The surplus, defined. The bread, safe.)*

scenes.synopsis: the de Varenne losses — the émigré principal, priced; the creditors, named.
scenes.prose:
> *(Octavia turns to the second column. "The de Varennes," she says. "Twelve hundred pounds of émigré money, entrusted to Elias in the bad years. He played it, covered the Hartwell losses first, and let the de Varennes fall." She writes the sum: £1,200. "Twelve hundred. The face sum — the loss was the keeping, and the keeping is priced in the paying." She glances at the trust's draft column. "The heirs receive it through the trust. Laurent's cousins in London. Quill knows the direction.")*
> *(Rose looks at the sum. Twelve hundred pounds. The price of a family's ruin, priced like a bill. "Who receives it?" "The heirs," Octavia says. "They become creditors, Rose. Not victims. Creditors get paid. That's the difference between charity and restitution." The principal, priced. The creditors, named.)*

scenes.synopsis: the de Valcourt acknowledgment — the third column, kept light; the boundary, honored.
scenes.prose:
> *(The third column is shorter, and Octavia keeps it so deliberately. "The de Valcourts," she says. "Twenty-eight hundred pounds — signed and promised in the spring. It stands outside the new structure; the trust acknowledges it, by name, and pays nothing new." She doesn't elaborate. She doesn't need to; the lightness is the point. Augusta's boundary, honored in the ledger's own hand. "Twenty-eight hundred," Rose repeats. "Already promised." "Already promised," Octavia confirms. "Light, as agreed.")*
> *(Rose nods. The kinship stays light. The husband's family's role stays unexamined. Whatever the de Valcourts lost, the ledger acknowledges it without narrating it, and that is precisely the mercy Augusta asked for. "Light," Rose says, "as agreed." Octavia turns the page. The column, closed. The boundary, kept.)*

scenes.synopsis: the total, stated — forty-one thousand six hundred pounds; the shape of the next ten years.
scenes.prose:
> *("Now the total," Octavia says. She writes it at the foot of the last page, in figures and then in words, the way her father taught her: £41,600. Forty-one thousand six hundred pounds. "Twenty-eight hundred promised in the spring, the de Valcourts. Thirty-eight thousand eight hundred to pay: eight thousand eight hundred now from the surplus (a hundred and fifty to Harrow, the rest to found the trust), and three thousand a year for ten years, from the canal." She looks up. "The Park's stones untouched. The roofs uncounted. The household's bread not in it.")*
> *(She closes the ledger, and the sound is final. "That's the price, Rose. The true price, counted precisely." A pause. "And now the affection." She takes Rose's hand, the mended glove and all. "It's the shape of the next ten years. Ten years of paying, and at the end of it, a clean ledger. No one can blackmail a paid debt. No one can print a settled account. It's worth it." Her eyes are bright. "You're worth it. The house is worth it. That's the affection. The precision was the easy part." The total, stated. The price, loved.)*

scenes.synopsis: the price, held — forty-one thousand six hundred pounds, turned over; the obstacle, examined.
scenes.prose:
> *(Alone after Octavia goes to wash the ink from her fingers, Rose holds the price. Forty-one thousand six hundred pounds. She turns it the way she turns everything: what it buys, what it costs, what it means. What it buys: Harrow's roof. The de Varennes as creditors. The de Valcourts, acknowledged lightly. A clean ledger in ten years. What it costs: eight thousand eight hundred now, three thousand a year. The canal's income, committed. The surplus, spent. What it means: the sin, paid for. Not hidden, not published — paid. She finds, examining it, that the price is not the obstacle. She expected to flinch at the sum. She doesn't flinch. The obstacle is elsewhere.)*
> *(The obstacle is the choosing. The price belongs to one door. The other two doors are free — expose costs nothing but the telling, bury costs nothing but the conscience. And yet the priced door is the one that keeps pulling at her, the way the ledger's weight pulled at her hand. Forty-one thousand six hundred pounds, and ten years, and a clean ledger. She sets the thought down beside the price. The choosing, nearer. The price, held.)*

scenes.synopsis: the law of restitution — Quill confirms the sums are payable; the trust, shaped.
scenes.prose:
> *(Quill comes at noon with his leather case, and Octavia's figures go into the solicitor's hands. He reads them twice, the way he reads everything, and nods. "Payable," he says. "The surplus is liquid, the canal income is steady, the sums are within the estate's means." He looks up. "The shape I'd recommend: a trust. The émigré trust, founded with the eight thousand eight hundred, fed by the canal's three thousand a year. Harrow's a hundred and fifty paid direct out of the founding sum — wages aren't trust business, they're debt business. His keeping, deeded by separate instrument." He writes the structure. "Ten years, and the trust dissolves, the ledger clean.")*
> *("And the de Valcourts?" "Outside it," Quill says, "as Octavia has it. The de Valcourt promise is already made, on its own paper, and will be paid on its own paper. Acknowledged in the founding paper, by name — not paid twice. Light." He closes his notebook. "One thing, Miss Hartwell. Restitution, once begun, is a public act. The trust's founding will be known. London will read it." "Let London read it," Rose says. "That's rather the point." Quill inclines his head. "Then it's sound law and sound sense." The trust, shaped. The law, satisfied.)*

scenes.synopsis: the counting-house — the two friends among the figures; fashion at the ledger.
scenes.prose:
> *(They take luncheon in the morning room with the ledger between them like a third guest, and Octavia, in her grey silk that predates the century, looks thoroughly at home among the figures. "You know," she says, "my father taught me accounting before he taught me dancing. He said a woman who can read a ledger can read anything." Rose looks at her friend: the precise hand, the bright eyes, the affection that does arithmetic. "And the dancing?" "The dancing," Octavia says, "was for the men. The ledger was for me.")*
> *(Rose wears the dove grey through luncheon, the pearls precise, the mended glove lifting the teacup. The counting-house has its own fashion: severity, clarity, the refusal to prettify a sum. She thinks about the forty-one thousand six hundred, the ten years, the clean ledger, and finds the numbers have a kind of beauty: the beauty of things exactly faced. "To the ledger," she says, lifting the cup. "To the ledger," Octavia says. "May it balance." The fashion, severe. The numbers, beautiful.)*

scenes.synopsis: Harrow, told he will be paid — the witness hears the price of his twenty years.
scenes.prose:
> *(She rides to the village at two, the ledger's figures in her memorandum book, because Harrow should hear it from her. He is at his table, the cloth over the papers, and she doesn't waste time. "A hundred and fifty pounds," she says. "Your wages. Paid at once. And your keeping, deeded." Harrow is quiet a long moment. Then: "A hundred and fifty." "A hundred and fifty," Rose confirms. "Octavia counted it. Quill approves it. It's —" she stops. "It's owed." He looks at the cloth over his papers. "Twenty years," he says quietly. "I stopped counting after five.")*
> *("There's more," Rose says. "The de Varennes. The de Valcourts. Forty-one thousand six hundred, all told, over ten years. From the surplus and the canal." She tells him the whole price, the trust, the ten years, the clean ledger. He listens completely, without moving. Then he says: "Your grandfather's sin, priced like a bill." "Priced like a debt," Rose corrects. "Debts get paid. That's the difference." Harrow nods slowly. "When?" "When I choose the door," Rose says. "The price belongs to the third door." "Then choose it," Harrow says. It is the simplest thing anyone has said all week.)*

scenes.synopsis: the dignity — Harrow's pride; wages vs. charity; the witness, paid as a man.
scenes.prose:
> *("Miss Hartwell," Harrow says, and the formality is back, which means the feeling is deep. "I need to ask. Is this —" he stops. "Is it wages, or is it kindness?" Rose understands at once. "Wages," she says firmly. "Counted by Octavia, in the ledger. It's owed." She takes out the memorandum book and shows him the column: his name, the years, the sum. "See? £150. Not a gift. An account." He studies the figures a long moment, and something in his shoulders does the thing shoulders do when a weight is recognized as legitimate.)*
> *("An account," he repeats. "Twenty years, and it's an account." He looks up. "Thank you," he says. "For the counting." She understands: the counting is the dignity. A gift would make him a beggar. An account makes him a creditor. "Your keeping too," she says. "Deeded. Yours." He is quiet. Then: "My mother's house sold for less than the wages." "Your mother's house," Rose says, "was in the wrong century." He laughs, startled, the dignity holding. The witness, priced as a man.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — THE ORDER: which creditors the trust pays first — Harrow, the émigrés, or all together; the paying, sequenced.
scenes.prose:
> *(Afternoon. Octavia's ledger is precise, and the total is fixed (forty-one thousand six hundred: the twenty-eight hundred promised, the thirty-eight thousand eight hundred to pay), but the order of the paying is Rose's to decide. Three orders offer themselves. Harrow first: the hundred and fifty now, his keeping deeded, the witness settled before anything else. The living debt, honored first. But Harrow is the smallest sum, and settling him first looks like buying the witness. The émigrés first: the de Varenne twelve hundred, the de la Roche nine hundred, the de Brissac fourteen hundred: the great sums, the ruined families, paid before the English creditors. The moral debt, honored first. But the émigré heirs are in London and Paris, and distant payments are slow. All together: the trust pays pro rata, no creditor preferred, Harrow and the heirs alike. The even hand. But even hands are slow hands, and Saturday's Pounce won't wait.)*
> *(She stands at the morning room table with the ledger open, and thinks of Octavia: the judgment is where the affection is. The order, chosen, becomes the trust's first instruction.)*
> *(The paying, ordered deliberately, the creditors' dignity in hand. The trust's first instruction was written. Whatever the order, the total stood: forty-one thousand six hundred, fixed.)*
